task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: What is dark matter, how do scientists know it exists, and why is it so hard to detect? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of February 20, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Dark matter is the name given to unseen mass inferred from gravitational effects observed throughout the universe; its physical nature has not been established.
Astronomers inferred unseen mass in the 1930s when surveys of galaxy cluster velocities showed galaxies in clusters moving too fast to be held together by the gravity of visible matter alone.

The strongest evidence comes from galaxy rotation curves: stars at the outer edges of spiral galaxies orbit at nearly the same speed as stars near the center, which requires far more mass than is visible.

The cosmic microwave background — the afterglow of the Big Bang, measured by satellites — provides a precise estimate that dark matter makes up approximately 27% of the universe's total energy-mass content; ordinary matter makes up only 5%.
Dark energy — a different, even more mysterious component — accounts for the remaining 68%; the three together constitute the standard cosmological model.

Physicist Dr. Anya Reinholt of Sandover Physics Institute said: "We know dark matter is there with the same confidence we know the floor is there when we step on it. We cannot see it. We feel the effect."

One class of candidate particles is called WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles; these hypothetical particles would interact with ordinary matter through gravity and the weak nuclear force but not through electromagnetism.

Despite decades of searching, no WIMP has been directly detected; several large underground detectors have ruled out progressively larger regions of the predicted mass and interaction rate parameter space.

Alternative candidates include axions (extremely light hypothetical particles), sterile neutrinos (a theoretical heavier sibling of known neutrinos), and primordial black holes left over from the early universe.
The liquid-xenon detectors described here operate deep underground to reduce cosmic-ray backgrounds that could mimic a particle signal; shielding materials include lead, water, and rock.
The Xenon-1T and LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiments use liquid xenon as a detection medium; a dark matter particle collision would produce a flash of light and a tiny electrical signal.
No confirmed dark matter signal has been recorded by any detector as of 2025; each null result narrows the parameter space but does not rule out dark matter's existence.

Modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) adjusts the gravity model rather than adding unseen mass. It can fit some galaxy-rotation observations but does not by itself account for all cluster measurements. In the Bullet Cluster, the mass inferred from gravitational lensing is separated from most of the hot, X-ray-emitting gas.

Dr. Reinholt said the null results have motivated theorists to propose lighter, more weakly interacting particles — sometimes called dark photons or fuzzy dark matter — that standard detectors are not optimized to find.
Gravitational lensing — the bending of light from distant galaxies by intervening mass — provides maps of dark matter distribution that match predictions from the standard model.
Computer simulations using the standard dark matter model accurately reproduce the large-scale structure of the universe, including the filaments and voids between galaxy clusters.
If dark matter consists of WIMPs that annihilate when they meet, space telescopes might detect the gamma rays produced; such signals have been searched for extensively without a confirmed detection.

Dr. Reinholt said the field is at an important juncture: either dark matter will be detected in the next generation of experiments, or physicists will need to fundamentally revise either the detector strategy or the standard model assumptions.
The Apex Dark Matter Observatory plans an upgraded xenon detector intended to be 40 times as sensitive as its current instrument. Construction is planned to begin in 2027 if funding is secured.
